name: Erik Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and down at the Hollins Estate yard by six. I've worked there twenty-two years as the stockman, so first job is the cattle: 140 head of beef, feeding, checking the calving shed, looking for anything off. Then it depends on the season, drilling barley in spring, baling in summer, fencing and muck-spreading in winter. I'm home for tea about six, and my partner Lena has usually beaten me back from the school kitchen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cattle, honestly. You get to know them, which cow will kick and which one calves without fuss. What wears me out is the forms and the new gadgets the estate keeps buying. They put a screen in the big John Deere that tells me where to drive, and I've driven that field since before the manager could walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let them keep their gadgets in the office. At the union branch meeting I'd probably make a joke that the robot uprising got cancelled. I'm not online much, I've still got a flip phone, so it would be the pub and the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my last eight years at Hollins look like the last twenty-two. I retire at 66, that's 2034, and the plan holds. The house is paid off and Lena and I have a decent pot put by, so I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep doing the calving rota and the feeding like always. I'd carry on putting the extra hundred a month into my workplace pension, which I started when our son left home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. I've watched three lots of new kit come in and out of that yard. If this one turns out to be another fad, I'd feel a bit smug, I'll admit that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still grumble about the screen in the tractor. If AI was a flop, they'd still have bought the thing, wouldn't they? The estate always buys first and asks the men after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Sami's an electrician and our daughter Noor's a nurse, so neither of them is sitting at a desk the software could take. I'd tell Sami that nothing much changed for the trades. I'd tell Noor the hospital will still need her hands at four in the morning.

say: I'd joke at the **union branch** that the robot uprising got cancelled.
I'd tell people the estate should keep its **gadgets** in the office, not the yard.
think: My **last eight years** at Hollins would look much like the last twenty-two.
With the house **paid off** and savings put by, my plan to retire at 66 holds.
do: Keep running the **calving rota** and the morning feed as normal.
Keep paying an **extra hundred** a month into the workplace pension.
feel: **Relieved**, and a bit smug that another fad came and went.
S0.quote: I've watched three lots of new kit come in and out of that yard.
fieldNote: His **security** comes from a paid-off house, savings and a fixed retirement date in 2034.
Distrust is aimed at the **estate's buying habits**, not at technology in general.
Sees both grown children in hands-on jobs and feels they're **out of reach** of software.

steps.text: Keep running the calving rota and morning feed at Hollins
Pay an extra hundred a month into the workplace pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the branch I'd say the union needs to get in early, before the estate decides who's surplus. I'd say it out loud at the pub too: when software does the thinking, the bosses keep the savings. That's always been the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, not much in the next few years. My job is hands in the muck, and the card says robots come slowly. The ones I'd worry about are Maureen in the estate office, who does the cattle passports and the orders, and the young lad who does the spraying records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring it up at the branch meeting in the first month and ask for a written promise on redeployment, not just a chat. I'd keep my head down and do my job. If they push me onto a tablet for the herd records, I'd ask Maureen to show me, and I'd moan the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own wage, more for the yard. It's like watching weather come in over the hill when you've already got your hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd moan the whole way. Would you actually use the tablet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the paper copy. I'd do the tablet because I'd have to, but I'd keep my own notebook in my coat pocket. My notebook has twenty-two years of calving dates, and no estate software is getting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen's 61 and has been in that office longer than I've been in the yard. If the estate's new software orders the feed and fills in the passports, she's the first one they let go. I'd stand next to her at any meeting, and I'd say so to the manager's face.

say: The **union** has to get in early, before the estate decides who's surplus.
When software does the thinking, the **bosses keep the savings**.
think: My own hands-on job looks **safe** for the next few years.
The **estate office** is where the cuts would land first, starting with Maureen.
do: Raise a **redeployment promise** at the first branch meeting.
Use the herd **tablet** only when forced, and keep his own paper notebook.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching bad weather come in after the hay's already in.
S1.quote: My notebook has twenty-two years of calving dates, and no estate software is getting it.
fieldNote: Speaks for colleagues, especially **Maureen in the office**, more than for himself.
Says he'd resist the tablet, then admits he'd **use it anyway** under protest.
His progressive view shows in who he **blames**: the estate owners, not the machines.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for a written redeployment promise for office staff
Keep feeding, calving and fencing as now at Hollins
Wait for the estate to say who it wants on the new software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal, and that it's the government's job to slow it down. The estate would sack the office by 2028 and the yard by 2031, and nobody would have planned a thing. At the branch I'd be pushing for a proper fight, not a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here's the honest sum. In 2031 I'm 63, three years short of my pension. A robot that can calve a heifer and mend a fence doesn't need a stockman, and the estate owners would buy one the week it's on sale. So I'd expect to be finished at Hollins three years early, and I'd lie awake over that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd put every spare pound into savings, not the holiday Lena wants in Portugal. Once AGI arrives in 2028 I'd go to the union and push for a deal: anyone over 60 gets paid through to pension age. I'd write to our MP too, which I've never done in my life. And I'd look at taking my pension early at 63, even on the reduced rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. It's not the money so much, we'd get by on what we've saved and Lena's wage. It's being told the job I've done my whole life can be done by a box on wheels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028, but the robots only around 2031. What happens in that gap for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those two years before the robots, while the office goes, would be the worst. You'd watch it coming for your own job and not be able to stop it. I'd be checking the farming papers every week for robot prices, which is daft for a man who won't use a smartphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena say to each other that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's school kitchen would probably keep going longer than my yard, because the card says the thinking stuff goes first and her job is hands-on too. She'd be the earner for a bit. I'd tell her straight that the Portugal trip waits, and she'd say I'm being dramatic, and we'd have a row about it at the kitchen table.

say: It's a **scandal**, and slowing it down is the government's job.
The union should fight for a **proper deal**, not sign a petition.
think: At **63** in 2031 I'd be finished at Hollins, three years short of my pension.
We'd manage on **savings** and Lena's wage, but I'd lie awake over it.
do: Save every spare pound now and **cancel** the Portugal holiday.
Push the union for **pay to pension age** for anyone over 60.
Write to the **MP** and look at taking his pension early at 63.
feel: **Sick** at being told a box on wheels can do his life's work.
Dread at watching the robot coming during the **three-year gap**.
S2.quote: A robot that can calve a heifer and mend a fence doesn't need a stockman, and the estate owners would buy one the week it's on sale.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** between AGI and robots feels to him like a slow countdown.
Money is a **cushion**, not the core fear; the core fear is losing his trade early.
A man who has never used AI plans to **watch robot prices** every week.

steps.text: Cancel the Portugal holiday and save every spare pound
Push the union for pay to pension age for workers over 60
Write to the MP asking for limits on farm robots
Take the workplace pension early at 63 if the yard goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, only louder: five years is enough time to make rules, so make them. The estate shouldn't be allowed to swap out its men without a plan. I'd say that at the branch and to anyone at the pub who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the dates fall nicely for me. The robots arrive around 2034, and that's the year I retire anyway. So I'd probably walk out the gate on my own terms, and it's the young lads on the estate who'd have the real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving the extra hundred, maybe push it to two hundred. I'd spend the five years making sure the union has a deal on paper for the younger ones before 2031. If the estate wants me to train the robot, I'd tell them where to put it, though I suppose I'd do it for a bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit guilty. I'd be fine and the lads wouldn't, and that doesn't sit right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum would worry me. He's good, and he'd have about seven years at the estate and then nothing in the yard. I'd tell Callum, our 24-year-old tractor driver, to get a trade on the side now, like my son Sami did with his electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd refuse to train the robot, but you'd do it for a bonus. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't square. I'm against the robots, but I'd train one for a bonus if it meant leaving with more money. I'd rather the bonus came to me than the estate kept it, put it that way.

say: Five years is **enough time** to make rules, so the government should make them.
The estate shouldn't swap out its men **without a plan**.
think: The robots land around **2034**, the same year I retire anyway.
The **young lads** on the estate would face the real problem.
do: Raise his pension top-up to **two hundred** a month.
Get a **union deal on paper** for younger workers before 2031.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **guilty** that he'd be fine and others wouldn't.
S3.quote: I'd tell Callum, our 24-year-old tractor driver, to get a trade on the side now, like my son Sami did with his electrics.
fieldNote: The **timing** suits him personally, which makes his worry turn outward.
Admits a **contradiction**: he'd train the robot for a bonus despite opposing it.
Names a specific younger worker, **Callum**, as the one at risk.

steps.text: Raise the pension top-up from one hundred to two hundred a month
Get a written union deal for younger estate workers before 2031
Keep working at Hollins until retiring in 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. Use it to set up proper retraining and a decent pension for farm workers. That's what I'd say at the branch, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means nothing in my working life. I'm gone from Hollins in 2034, and robots don't come until around 2039, when I'm 71. The thinking AI in 2036 hits the estate office, not my yard, and I'll be out of both by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on. Same rota, same pension plan, retire at 66. I'd vote for whoever promises to tax the robot owners and pay for training, which is who I vote for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, if I'm truthful. I'd feel sorry for whoever's in my boots in 2039, but it won't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you picture yourself in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in the garden and doing a bit of relief milking for the neighbours if they'd still have me. I'd probably watch a robot drive past the estate fence and feel glad I got out in time. Lena says I'll be bored stiff in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, my grandkids would be old enough to choose. I'd tell my granddaughter Leila to learn something that needs a person in the room, nursing like her mum or a trade like her uncle Sami. Not an office, that's the first to go.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so use it for retraining and **pensions** for farm workers.
Don't waste the decade arguing; **plan** for the people in the yard.
think: I'm out of Hollins in **2034**, years before the robots arrive.
The **thinking AI** in 2036 hits the estate office, not my yard.
do: Carry on with the **same rota** and retire at 66 as planned.
Vote for whoever will **tax robot owners** to pay for training.
feel: **Calm** for himself, with some sympathy for whoever stands in his boots.
S4.quote: I'd probably watch a robot drive past the estate fence and feel glad I got out in time.
fieldNote: The ten-year warning puts the robots **five years after** his planned retirement.
Turns his attention to his **grandchildren's** choices and away from his own job.
His politics stay **steady**; he votes the same way in every picture.

steps.text: Keep the same rota at Hollins and retire at 66 in 2034
Vote for candidates who would tax robot owners to fund training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no contest. It lands the robots in my yard three years before my pension, and it gives nobody time to sort a deal. What would help is a law that says a worker over 60 who loses his job to a machine gets paid through to pension age, out of the machine owner's pocket.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the whole thing to me. If the estate owns the robots, the estate gets richer and the village gets emptier. If the workers or the council had a share, I'd hate them a lot less.

headlineQuote: If the estate owns the robots, the estate gets richer and the village gets emptier.
portrait: A **58-year-old stockman** on the Hollins Estate for 22 years, with a paid-off house and savings.
Never uses AI and keeps a **paper notebook** of calving dates in his coat pocket.
Sees **union deals** and laws as the answer, and blames estate owners, not machines.
Calm when robots arrive after his **2034 retirement**, alarmed when they come at 63.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would end his job three years before his pension.
whatWouldHelp: A law paying workers over 60 who lose jobs to machines **through to pension age**.
Workers or the council owning **a share** of the robots, not just the estate.
